newsitem.title: USA: Dispute over Boutros-Ghali spices Clinton UN trip.
newsitem.headline: Dispute over Boutros-Ghali spices Clinton UN trip.

text.p: The public highlight of President Bill Clinton's United Nations visit on Tuesday will be a speech applauding a nuclear test ban treaty, but most U.N.-watchers will focus on an intriguing political sub-plot.

That is Clinton's crusade to dump Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali as secretary-general of the world organisation, and how the two handle personal encounters when the president visits U.N. headquarters in New York City to promote the prospective, sweeping test ban accord.

Washington's commitment to ousting Boutros-Ghali is driven by widespread suspicion among Americans that the United Nations is an expensive bureaucracy that has stumbled badly in global hotspots like Somalia and Bosnia.
There are sure to be smiles aplenty when Clinton and Boutros-Ghali meet, but White House officials warn against taking polite outward appearances at face value.

"The president has made an irrevocable decision on the need to find a new secretary-general who can more actively spearhead the reform process in the U.N. There is no backing off on that. It's a done deal," one official said.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the administration is consulting with other nations on a replacement for Boutos-Ghali, and has no firm candidate at present.

Clinton, in the midst of a soaring re-election campaign in which U.S. membership in the United Nations has not surfaced as much of an issue, will address the U.N. general assembly after signing the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty.
Approved by the general assembly two weeks ago by a vote of 158-3, with India, Libya and tiny Bhutan opposed, the treaty bans nuclear explosions in the atmosphere, underground or anywhere else.

"The treaty fulfils a dream first espoused by President Dwight Eisenhower and given life by President John Kennedy, with the limited test ban treaty," a White House official said. "President Clinton will emphasise that it moves us significantly away from the nuclear precipice."
The agreement must be ratified by 44 nations with nuclear power capability before it enters into force but the consent of eight countries is crucial.

They are the five acknowledged nuclear powers -- the United States, Britain, France, Russia and China -- and three so-called threshold states believed capable of developing nuclear weapons quickly: India, Pakistan and Israel.
According to a senior Clinton administration official, none of the eight countries will allow the treaty to enter into force until the other seven are ready to ratify it.

India, which exploded a bomb in 1974, vows to block it from taking force. It maintains the treaty is flawed because it does not commit the nuclear powers to eventually destroy their arsenals, and in fact lets them develop more sophisticated means of testing without explosions.

New Delhi is also worried about China's nuclear capability and that of its neighbour and regional power rival Pakistan, which the United States said has received nuclear weapons-making equipment from China.
Clinton, who will campaign in New Jersey later on Tuesday, intends to stress the positive in his speech, officials said.
In a campaign speech in California the day after the treaty was approved, he said conclusion of the pact showed that "we are making this a safer world."

Clinton plans one key meeting on the fringes of his U.N. visit, a brief get-together with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto at the U.S. mission in New York. The two last met at the G7 summit in France in June.
"This meeting will be brief, but the leaders will touch on a range of issues we deal with together, including trade and security relations," a U.S. official said.
